title: Recording the four-altos album with Zoot Sims
summary: Zoot recorded free choruses, then Handy wrote harmony parts and Zoot overdubbed them.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Anyway, I figured out how to do it which is how we did it and we did it in this manner. I wrote charts in which the first chorus

was created, a melody by me, and written out. Then I followed this with choruses of free blowing, or I may have written a chorus of free blowing, then put in something I wanted him to play, wrote something for four bars and then gave him some more free blowing, for another chorus or more, then I put in a final statement which he had to play and an ending.

We went into the studio with this type of chart, Zoot and a rhythm section, and he read the first chorus, which we all played our parts, he blew through the jazz sections, read the interval part, did some more free blowing on his jazz sections and then read the last part out.

I took the tape home--I did this with I don't know how many tunes there were-- I think there were eight or ten different tunes-- I did this with every tune. Now I took the tape home and copied off all of his free blowing choruses. I wrote them down and then I wrote a second part to his first part, a third part

and a fourth part, matching his free blowing. Then he went back into the studio after I had written this, added the other three horns with a pair of earphones. He was alone with just a pair of earphones, reading these extra parts, and as each part was added onto the previous one, we wound up with the sound I wanted, Zoot himself playing free blowing, perfect harmony.
How many takes did this all take?

It took a little doing, it took a little time, a lot of patience. One of the problems we discovered was that Zoot would come across passages that he had played, that he couldn't read and breathe properly. When he blew it free on the record, he played a thing eight bars long without taking a breath, but to read it he found it very difficult and he had to learn to prepare himself for it, so that he could get the whole thing out in one breath. Of course each time he would lose
This was obviously the first time Zoot had ever seen his own work on notes in front?
Did he respond in any way to that?
I think what he did was sensational. I don't think too many people could have done it.

The idea was to have the results sound genuine and not read, and of course the lead of it was exactly that. The fact that the other parts were read added on so well was a testament to his own beautiful virtuosity.
